source.title: A survey detection channel overrides the pixels in an astronomical foundation model, and biases tomographic mean redshifts

record.tranche_reason: The paper evaluates sparse dictionaries as steering handles for a detection gate, not whether SAE reconstruction error is structured or predictable in the ways claimed.
record.gate_note: The study reports SAE reconstruction FVU and steering recovery, but does not analyze whether the residual is linearly predictable, how error norms scale across SAE sizes, or whether SAE errors fall on the same contexts. The SAE results below are recorded as related findings with versions ["none"].
record.test_reason: The study trains BatchTopK SAEs on AION-1 block-6 activations and asks whether gate-selective SAE features steer a detection gate better than difference-in-means or PCA. It never analyses the SAE error vector. There is no linear prediction of the error from the input, no per-token error norms across sizes, no loss comparison of spliced-in reconstructions against random errors, and no test of whether keeping the error term matters for steering or circuits. It reports aggregate FVU, but aggregate reconstruction quality cannot show any version's effect. It does not cite the original dark-matter paper. 'Discusses' is a loose fit: it is a tangential SAE-evaluation study with no test or use of the claim.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct, with one completion. Under the same conditions, the authors also conclude that SAEs are beaten on average by difference-in-means and on average and at best by PCA, so they 'do not earn their cost' for this target. They also conclude that single-seed causal evaluations of dictionaries are uninformative.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains BatchTopK dictionaries on AION-1 block-6 activations and evaluates their causal steering of a detection gate; it does not measure SAE error predictability or compare error structure across scales.
record.method_sensitivity: Steering recovery varies with dictionary width, sparsity k, and seed; the paper reports seed-only differences up to 18.4 percentage points.

fits_no_version.finding: Across 15 BatchTopK SAEs, steering recovery at α=4 ranged from 26.0% to 74.7%. All beat random (13.4%); only two beat difference-in-means (64.3%) and one beat matched-k PCA. Seed alone moved recovery by up to 18.4 points.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE-feature steering directions are unreliable, seed-sensitive causal handles compared with simple linear baselines.

fits_no_version.finding: SAE FVU (0.023–0.067) is far below matched-k PCA FVU (0.149–0.350), yet FVU does not predict steering recovery. The best reconstructor (FVU 0.023) recovers 53.5%; the best steerer (FVU 0.067, 10.5% latents alive) recovers 74.7%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE reconstruction quality does not predict causal steering utility.

fits_no_version.finding: At fixed k, FVU does not fall monotonically with width; the 32768-wide SAEs reconstruct worse than the 8192-wide ones. This coincides with low fractions of live latents (10.5–52.4% at width 32768, versus 51.6–99.1% at 8192). The alive percentages are in Table 8 but are not recorded in the rows.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In this sweep, wider BatchTopK SAEs had more dead latents and higher aggregate reconstruction error. This is a training-quality effect on total error, not on error structure.

record.problems: The dictionary sweep is restricted to one model, one layer, and one causal target; the authors state that dictionary training is not bit-reproducible and that the seed spread includes run-to-run nondeterminism. The study does not evaluate the claim's dark-matter error properties.

untested.parts: Whether SAE error is linearly predictable from the input activation; not measured.

Per-token error-norm predictability, and whether larger SAEs fail on the same contexts. Only aggregate FVU per width is given: nonzero at all widths and non-monotone (k=16: 0.065/0.052/0.067). This is not a scaling analysis of error.
Downstream loss when reconstructions are spliced in, compared with random errors of the same norm; not measured.
Decomposition of the error into linear and nonlinear parts, and whether either part is learnable; not measured.
Steering uses SAE-feature directions added at matched norm. There is no comparison with and without the error term, so loss of behaviour attributable to the error is not measured.
Dark matter as a training artifact; architectures and objectives are not compared. Dead-latent fractions are reported but not tied to error structure.

missing.what: The per-dictionary fraction of live latents (Alive %) is not captured. It bears on the dead-latent explanation of reconstruction error, though not on any version directly.

record.verdict_notes: Rows are correctly linked to ['none'] with state cannot_determine. The PCA FVU and the difference-in-means/PCA recovery figures are proper baselines; the rows report the SAE values against them. Each steering row's baseline field holds several baselines; that is acceptable. This is a single model, layer and target, with non-bit-reproducible training. Most of the paper (detection gate, tokeniser, redshift) is unrelated to the phenomenon.

versions.untested_parts: Whether a large share of SAE error is a linear function of input activations.
Whether per-token SAE error norms are predictable across SAE sizes, larger SAEs fail on the same contexts, or error persists with scale.
Whether SAE reconstruction errors harm model loss more than random errors of the same size.
Whether linear error corresponds to unlearned features and nonlinear error is qualitatively distinct or resists further dictionary learning.
Whether SAE feature-based circuits or steering omit a meaningful share of model behaviour unless the error term is retained.
Whether dark matter is an SAE-training artifact or shrinks with improved architectures or end-to-end training.
